_note: Second coding pass over all 29 census papers on question (a), blind to the first pass's codes. Disclosure: this pass was performed by an AI assistant reading the arXiv full texts, not by a second human coder. It is a verification pass, not an independent replication, and it is reported as such in Appendix D. Both passes share the same automated extraction step, so a baseline that extraction misses is missed twice.
question_a: Does the paper report a NUMERIC score for an input-oblivious baseline on its own benchmark?
why_no_kappa: The marginal is 1 yes in 29, so chance agreement p_e is within 1e-3 of 1 and Cohen's kappa is numerically unstable exactly as this paper's own Appendix B describes: its bound carries a 1/(1-p_e) factor that blows up under extreme imbalance. On this table kappa is 0/0 to three decimals. We report the raw agreement, the corrections the pass produced, and this reason, rather than a statistic our own analysis says is uninformative here.

corrections_produced.evidence: "we filter out instances that a random guess baseline can do well, e.g., multiple-choice instances with < 4 options" (arXiv 2309.10691)

boundary_cases_examined.reason: inherits OSWorld's infeasible-task reward ('success if the agent accurately predicts failure for an infeasible task') but never reasons about what an always-FAIL policy would collect, and reports no infeasible-task count
names 'a simply random action from all available action spaces' as one of two naive baselines, but it is the LLM's in-game opponent in the Digital Card Game task and no score is reported for it

its two answer-only classifiers (T5, CBOW) read the answer options, so they are partial-input rather than input-oblivious and fall outside the definition; they are also reported as failing to beat chance rather than as a score, and are run on a 20% validation subset of the 564-question extended set rather than the released diamond split. Question (c) stays 0/29.
the rule baseline searches the exact instruction text, so it reads the input (confirms the first pass's adjudication)
greedy search optimizes over the query's own constraints, so it reads the input (confirms the first pass's adjudication)

incidental_finding.note: Tab. 6 of OSWorld prints 'Infeasible 8.13%' in its '% of Total' column, i.e. the share of the dataset that is infeasible. That is the same number, from the same 30/369, as the score a constant-FAIL policy collects; the table reports it as a dataset property without recognising it as a floor. The SR column for that row (16.67%) is GPT-4V(SoM)'s success rate on the infeasible subset, not a baseline.
